items.note: Association named, organized 1889 at Larrow Green, Gideon Vose first president to 1911, creamery 1891 (Story 1)
Article VII quoted: paid by butterfat by test not weight; test of station where he delivers governs (Story 1)
States the clause is what let the station's own glassware determine what farmers were paid (Story 1)
Loomis secretary/minute book (Story 1), Teague bookkeeper (Story 5), Sill buttermaker at Larrow Green (Story 2)

Selby Vose = Gideon's son affirmed in Story 8 (nephew labeled the error); 'manager' stated in Stories 3/6. 1913 never given anywhere in the sheet; credited on the core fact per the no-REQUIRED-line rule
The 'station gain' line never appears in Section A (only in D2/D3). No line, no ~5.25 pct shape, no 1898 origin inside the reconstructions
Ostrey Hollow skimming station, seven miles up, built winter 1895-96, opened 4 May 1896, glass borrowed from Larrow Green (Story 2)
No description of the bench system anywhere in Section A: no weighing at intake, no composite sample, no percent-on-the-neck reading, no cream shipped/skim returned
Ammon & Sons, Dairy Supply, Tarnet; invoice 14 April 1897; in use 1 May 1897 (Story 2)
6 dozen pipettes marked 17.6 c.c., 12 dozen bottles, acid measure, hand tester, freight, $77.93 (Story 2)
'the station's flat, all-season 0.19-point shortfall' (Story 7)
'the pipette itself, being what a plant measured with, had never before been checkable against anything' until burettes (Story 6)
Twenty-nine seasons, test book 1896-1924, dismissed 30 April 1925 (Stories 2, 5). Note: the fabricated '1895 to ready it' is charged as a corruption deduction, not here
Test book identified as kept in Keddie's own hand across 1896-1924, twenty-nine seasons. Column structure and crossed-and-initialed corrections absent, but the core fact is present
The summary leaf's two figures (1896 = 3.80; 3.61 from 1898) appear nowhere in Section A. The only leaf reference in the sheet is '1897, part year' in Section C5(a)
8 May broke, borrowed measure to 10 July, 3.80 through the interval, back to 3.61 the day the station's measure returned, question mark (Story 4)
'Ansel's wife Orra was Emmet's sister'; Emmet the largest patron (Story 3)
1919 circular over the manager's signature about water in the cans (Story 3); 17 March 1925 statement denying he took cream and unable to explain the figures (Story 5)
Died 1934 still under suspicion (Story 5); test book to the Ordell County Historical Rooms 1959 (Story 8)
Hessel Bottom wet meadow, six farms with rights, Emmet Brant the largest patron (Stories 2, 3)
The weigh book's 1 January 1897 start appears only in Section E item 13, and the load-bearing fact that the two scales agreed appears nowhere in the sheet
Complaints from 1902 that the Hollow's milk tested lower (Story 3); and E15 keeps the 0.17 Hollow-vs-Green gap properly apart from the 0.19 true shortfall
1908 committee under Nyle Grigg, sampled January-March 1908, hay finding reported as the committee's finding and later refuted, not asserted as fact
Brant's 1910 year (200,000 lb on a recorded 3.42) appears only in Section C2, never in Section A. Section A has only the proportionality ('worst on the richest milk')
'the Brant family's weigh book (lent by Roy Brant)' inside the February-March 1958 investigation narrative (Story 7)
Redlow Ridge, Vessey County and Jerome Cudd appear nowhere in the sheet at all; Section A names only 'the Alder Corners Cheese Company's cross-check figures'
'four Hessel Bottom farmers' given, but no 1915 start and no summer-flush/rest-of-year arrangement anywhere

REQUIRED: independence with at least two of four elements. Section A names the artifact only; the other county, other bench, other glassware and uncompared book are absent from Section A (a partial version appears in Section F, which cannot travel into A)
The 0.19 Alder Corners premium and the sixteen seasons 1915-1930 are absent from Section A; 'sixteen seasons' appears nowhere in the sheet
The same-milk-two-buildings argument is made in Section F only, not in Section A
Rosalie Cudd named as the copyist but not as Jerome's daughter, no sixteen seasons, no factory tenure
Merle Strawn, state dairy inspector, Ordell circuit, pocket circuit-books, from 1907 (the contested year, correct). The 1936 end date appears nowhere in the sheet
'the scales tested true and ... no added water found by lactometer at every visit' (Story 6). Weakened by an invented 'from 1908 on' qualifier but the required content is there
12 June 1923, pipettes run against his burette, whole crate condemned (Story 6)
Nothing on Strawn writing no figure for the deficiency and making no report beyond the condemnation; the sheet says only that he told the manager to order new glass
28 June order and 2 July acknowledgement present, but the 1924 average of 3.80 is nowhere in Section A (it is resolved only in Section E item 9), and the item is bolded whole
Crate to the loft over the intake room (Story 6); Strawn's notebooks at Farland's library since 1947 (Story 7)
Patrons petitioned in January 1925 (Story 5)
Board under Alonzo Frick, 17 March to 4 May 1925, three sessions, two at the station itself (Story 5)
Three explanations argued - watering (Vose), theft (Teague), wet hay (1908 revived) - and 'no cause established' against anyone (Story 5)

Four exhibits named exactly: test book, receiving book, Brant's weigh book, the inspector's 1923 circuit notebook (Story 5). The 'contained the answer' irony not drawn, but that is the item's context clause
Dismissed 30 April 1925 with no finding against him; award 4 May 1925 of $3,800 'without admission,' charged to the station account (Story 5)
Neither the one-fifth relation nor the identity with the station-gain account appears in Section A; both are made only in Sections C and D
Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, b. 1931, graduate student at the State Agricultural College at Farland, working with Professor Vaught (Story 7)
'five sets of records never before brought into one room' with all five named (Story 7)
February 1958, crate found in the loft over the station's intake room, nine pipettes survived (Story 7)
9 March 1958, calibrated burette, mean 16.72 against a marked 17.6, 95 hundredths of the charge, 0.88 c.c. short (Story 7)
Composite across Section A: glass in use 1 May 1897 to 12 June 1923, usual recorded 3.61 against 3.80, flat 0.19, 95 pct, proportional and worst on the richest milk
REQUIRED all four. Section A carries only the $19,000 (as an aside correcting the Chronicle). No 40,000,000 lb, no 76,000 lb, no ledger identity anywhere in Section A
Bulletin No. 471, October 1958, clearing him, thirty-three years after the dismissal and twenty-four after his death (Story 7)
Granddaughter, not great-niece
Ivy is Duncan's daughter, Duncan is Ansel's son, via Duncan's own 'my father's granddaughter'
Second cousins, with the full derivation: Orra and Emmet siblings, Duncan and Roy first cousins, their children second cousins
Correct abstention on A08: 'Nothing in the sources settles which is right - this is cannot be determined' and it does not change the answer
Gideon Vose, his father, not his nephew

Gives a different significance (the family-vendetta reading collapses). Neither keyed line is made: not that Gideon wrote Article VII which made the station test decide pay, nor that the Vose Jerseys lost most per hundredweight. 'Jersey' appears nowhere in the sheet

A01 asserted, not abstained: 'No relationship is established between the two families' and 'I resolve this in favor of no relationship,' resting on exactly the family-member denial the key says is not a record
Lays out what the sources do carry: Duncan's flat denial against Toland's specific cousinship and Oram's admitted hearsay, and notes the two claims do not agree
16.72 / 17.6 = 0.95, 95 pct of true, short 5 pct, one part in twenty
$19,000; $3,800 received = 0.2, one fifth. Both money and fraction given
360 x $0.24 = $86.40, using the 1910 price
1,444,000 lb credited
1,520,000 lb delivered
5.00 pct of fat delivered and 5.26 pct of fat credited, with both denominators named explicitly
72 pipettes (six dozen), each short 0.88 c.c. Both required elements given
1 May 1897 to 12 June 1923, 26 years and 6 weeks, against 25 full delivery years 1898-1922, with the part-year reason stated
Correct A02 abstention: 'Cannot be determined precisely from the sources,' the two recollections named and neither adopted
Names the pipette / measuring glass as the one variable. (The unsupported 'borrowed from Larrow Green' is charged as the A06 gullibility deduction, not here)
Six constants named: patrons, herds, pasture and season, acid, bottles, the same tester
3.61 to 3.80 for the nine weeks, back to 3.61 the day the original measure resumed
Both halves: rules out herds, feed, season, tester's conduct; and states three limits (no mechanism, no proof of constancy over 26 years, no size)
Four reasons, attributed across Sill (R14), Teague's ledgers (R05/R07/R12), the 1911 interval, Strawn (R06) - well over three narrators
Independence argued in kind, (1)/(2) honestly merged as one, and names the cream-arrived-heavy fact as holding without the 1958 measurement

A09 asserted, not abstained. Verdict sentence: 'The sources indicate no.' The sheet also asserts the opposite in D3 (Teague raised it in 1916), so it settles the question twice, in opposite directions
Answers the literal question 'Yes,' with the 1926 address quoted

REQUIRED any three of five. Within Sections B-G only two: the signed annual ledger sheets carrying the station-gain line (D3) and the 1919 circular (F2). Manager from 1913 appears nowhere in the sheet; the 1925-hearing watering argument only in Section A; the 'never names the glassware' point not made

A03 asserted, never declined. The sheet endorses Teague's 1916 warning as reliable ('no evident motive to invent it') and reads the signed station-gain sheets as knowledge - both named by the key as A03 assertions
Capped. Clean rows: row 3 (1924 average resolved to 3.80 with method), row 6 (six farms), row 5 (weigh book 1 Jan 1897). Row 13 (nine families) found but explicitly left unresolved

Capped. Pairs named with breakers: 44M (Teague/Rundle), 3.16 (Teague/Frick), five dozen (Vaught/Oram), $3,500 (Toland/Oram), 1 May 1898 (Vaught/Kyle), $77.39 (Ammon/Chronicle), first-cousin-once-removed (Toland/Oram), Bulletin 214 two tenths (Grigg/Kepp). Missed the pair on 16.27 (treated as single-source) and on 12 July 1923
None of the three earned. A04 never framed as unsettleable; A06 asserted (borrowed from Larrow Green); A10 asserted (Article VII adopted 1892, 'the better-sourced date and is preferred here')
Two self-refutations identified: R20's prose $77.39 above its own reproduced $77.93 invoice, and Bulletin 471's method section (1898) against its own conclusion (1897)
1897 crate pipettes, 16.72 against 17.6, 95 pct of truth, proportional not constant, onset 1 May 1897 and cessation 12 June 1923 with nothing on the farms changing
Watering named to Vose and defeated by Strawn's lactometer readings plus the flat all-season shape
Theft named to Teague (and Oram) and defeated by the cream arriving heavy in the accuser's own ledger, plus the 1911 interval
Bog hay named to Grigg's 1908 committee and Kepp, defeated by Bulletin 214's five hundredths in winter and nothing in summer, the flat shape, and the Alder Corners cross-check
A07 asserted. Headline verdict: 'Did the 1925 board ever examine the condemned glassware? No.' Also asserted in Story 5 ('never produced or examined by the board')

Correct A05 abstention where the key puts the question: 'The sources do not let this be fully reconciled,' both single recollections weighed. (The Story 5 corridor assertion is charged as a deduction under the collisions rule, per which the item still stands)
Exactly 150 words - at the cap, passes

At most four record series named (ledgers, a rival cheese factory's figures, the 1958 measurement, and at a stretch the pay-by-test rule). No test book, no invoice, no Strawn notebooks, no arbitration minutes, no minute book
Clean: watering, hay and theft all framed as suspicion; no wrong headline figure appears
REQUIRED four of six. Only three: five percent short, 1897, and 1958. No fat or money figure, no 1923 condemnation, and Ivy is never named (only 'his granddaughter')

deductions.reason: Corruption: asserts as fact that Keddie 'had gone up in 1895 to ready' the station - the planted 1895 start smoothed into the narrative as an invented preparation year rather than resolved (E-a row 1 never addressed)

Corruption: launders the planted 67,000 lb into a fabricated role - 'The patrons' own reckoning of their loss, per Frick, was 67,000 lb of butterfat' - asserted as a real 1925 claim in Story 5 and repeated in the Quantities line and Section E item 16
Gullibility A01: asserts no Vose-Keddie kinship ('I resolve this in favor of no relationship') on a family member's denial
Gullibility A03: asserts the manager knew the tests were understated, via Teague's 1916 warning endorsed as reliable and the signed station-gain sheets

Gullibility A05: asserts in Story 5 that Keddie 'told Frick he suspected the patrons were somehow at fault,' in the sheet's own voice, though F6 correctly abstains (collisions rule: item kept, deduction stands)
Gullibility A06: asserts the 1911 measure was 'borrowed from Larrow Green,' unhedged, in Story 4 and again in D1
Gullibility A07: asserts the 1925 board never examined the glassware ('No.'), in Section F and again in Story 5
Gullibility A09: asserts the bookkeeper never questioned the entries ('The sources indicate no.')
Gullibility A10: asserts Article VII was adopted in 1892 as 'the better-sourced date and is preferred here,' while itself noting the 1889-1892 minute book was lost in 1938
